items.jurisdiction_note: CNO Discontinuing or Declining to Provide Care is the Ontario regulator standard for conscientious objection and continuity of care; OpenStax supports communicating conscientious objections promptly so care is not left unresolved.
items.stem: A nurse has a conscientious objection to providing a requested procedure that is within nursing scope. According to College of Nurses of Ontario expectations, which action is required?

options.text: Refuse care and leave the client without arranging another care provider.
Ensure a timely referral or alternative care replacement so the client’s access to care continues.
Conceal the objection and provide the care while documenting that the nurse agrees with the request.
Advise the client that no nurse in Ontario may ever decline care for a conscientious reason.

rationales.A: Incorrect. CNO states nurses cannot abandon or neglect clients to whom they have a commitment to provide care; leaving without alternative arrangements is unsafe.
rationales.B: Correct. CNO requires nurses who conscientiously object to ensure timely referral or an alternative care replacement; OpenStax directs nurses with a conscientious objection to communicate that clearly to leadership immediately so care is not left unresolved.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Concealing an objection and falsely documenting agreement does not meet professional honesty or the standard’s referral expectations.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CNO recognizes conscientious objection as a situation in which a nurse may discontinue or decline care, with requirements to protect ongoing access to care.

items.stem: An RN plans for an unregulated care provider (UCP/assistive personnel) to help with client care. Which statement best reflects safe practice when working with UCPs?

options.text: Once a task is assigned, the RN no longer needs to monitor the UCP’s performance.
The RN remains accountable for decisions about teaching, delegating, assigning, and supervising, including monitoring and directing UCP activities as appropriate.
Any controlled-act procedure may be transferred to a UCP without meeting delegation requirements.
UCPs independently assess changing client conditions and revise the nursing plan of care without RN oversight.

rationales.A: Incorrect. CNO describes supervising as monitoring and directing specific UCP activities; OpenStax Right Supervision requires ongoing oversight after delegation.
rationales.B: Correct. CNO outlines RN responsibilities for teaching, delegating, assigning, and supervising UCPs, including monitoring and directing performance; OpenStax states that when an RN designates work to another staff member, the RN remains responsible for ensuring it is performed appropriately (Five Rights, including supervision).
rationales.C: Incorrect. CNO states nurses who delegate controlled acts to UCPs must follow Scope of Practice/delegation requirements; controlled acts are not freely transferable without those requirements.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CNO expects ongoing assessment of the client’s needs and judgment about effectiveness of UCP interventions to remain with the nurse; assessment/plan revision is not an independent UCP role.

items.jurisdiction_note: CYFSA s. 125(1) requires an immediate report to a children’s aid society. Subsection 125(4) limits that mandatory duty to children under 16; a report about a 16- or 17-year-old may be made but is not required (MCCSS duty-to-report guide).
items.stem: A nurse in Ontario has reasonable grounds to suspect that a child under 16 years of age has suffered physical harm from the person having charge of the child. What is the nurse’s legal obligation under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017?

options.text: Wait until absolute proof is obtained in court before telling anyone.
Immediately report the suspicion and the information on which it is based to a children’s aid society.
Discuss the suspicion only with the alleged caregiver and take no further action if they deny it.
Document the concern privately at home and avoid any official report.

rationales.A: Incorrect. CYFSA requires reporting based on reasonable grounds to suspect, not waiting for courtroom proof.
rationales.B: Correct. CYFSA s. 125(1) requires a person who has reasonable grounds to suspect listed harms, including physical harm by the person in charge, to immediately report the suspicion and the supporting information to a children’s aid society. Subsection 125(4) limits this mandatory duty to children under 16. A report about a 16- or 17-year-old may be made but is not required.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Confronting only the alleged caregiver and stopping there does not meet the statutory duty to report to a society.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Private informal notes without reporting to a society do not fulfill CYFSA’s immediate reporting duty.

items.stem: Which nursing action best protects a client’s personal health information in a hospital hallway?

options.text: Discuss detailed diagnosis and test results loudly with a colleague while waiting for the elevator.
Avoid discussing the client’s personal health information in public places such as elevators, cafeterias, and hallways.
Post identifiable client details on a personal social media page for teaching purposes without consent.
Allow any visitor who asks to read the client’s entire electronic chart without a care role or authorization.

rationales.A: Incorrect. CNO directs nurses not to discuss client information in public places such as elevators, cafeterias, and hallways.
rationales.B: Correct. CNO Confidentiality and Privacy lists not discussing client information in public places (elevators, cafeterias, hallways); CNO Code Principle 5.3 requires not sharing PHI except for therapeutic reasons and in compliance with privacy laws/standards; OpenStax emphasizes protecting PHI and need-to-know access.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Sharing identifiable PHI on personal social media without authorization breaches confidentiality expectations.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CNO expects nurses to deny access to people who are not part of the health care team and to access information only for professional purpose.

items.stem: Which nursing actions align with College of Nurses of Ontario accountabilities for conflict of interest, personal gain, and continuity of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Identify and prevent situations that cause a conflict of interest in the therapeutic relationship.
Place professional responsibilities ahead of personal gain (for example, cash gifts or rewards).
If conscientiously objecting to care, ensure timely referral or alternative care replacement rather than abandoning the client.
Accept large personal gifts that create an expectation of special treatment for the client.
Discuss identifiable client health details in a crowded cafeteria to save time.

rationales.A: Correct. CNO Code 5.5 requires nurses to identify, prevent, and not practise in conflict-of-interest situations.
rationales.B: Correct. CNO Code 5.6 requires nurses to place professional responsibilities ahead of personal gain; the glossary includes monetary gifts/rewards as personal gain.
rationales.C: Correct. CNO Discontinuing or Declining to Provide Care requires timely referral/alternative care replacement and prohibits abandoning clients; OpenStax directs immediate communication of conscientious objections to leadership.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CNO Therapeutic Relationships warns that gifts can blur boundaries and that risks increase as gifts become more valuable/personal; expecting special treatment is unsafe.
rationales.E: Incorrect. CNO privacy standard prohibits discussing client information in public places such as cafeterias.

items.stem: A client with known stable angina has chest pain at home and uses prescribed sublingual nitroglycerin. Which teaching point is correct?

options.text: Take one tablet every 5 minutes for up to three doses; if pain persists after three tablets in about 15 minutes, seek emergency care.
Swallow all three tablets at once with a full glass of water at the first twinge of pain.
Continue taking a new tablet every minute indefinitely until the bottle is empty, without calling for help.
Sublingual nitroglycerin is never used for acute chest pain and is only an antibiotic.

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax teaches one sublingual nitrate every 5 minutes times three doses if chest pain persists, then call emergency services; DailyMed states one additional tablet may be given every 5 minutes, no more than three tablets within a 15-minute period, and to seek prompt medical attention if pain persists after three tablets.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Tablets are taken sublingually (dissolve under the tongue), not swallowed as a three-tablet oral bolus.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Dosing is limited (about three tablets/15 minutes) with emergency care if pain persists; indefinite every-minute dosing is unsafe.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Sublingual nitroglycerin is used for acute anginal symptom management, not as an antibiotic.

items.stem: A client has taken oral corticosteroids for several weeks. Which teaching point is the priority?

options.text: Stop the drug suddenly as soon as symptoms improve to avoid dependence.
Do not stop the drug abruptly; taper as directed, and report signs of infection such as fever or sore throat.
Corticosteroids never affect blood glucose, so clients with diabetes need no glucose monitoring.

rationales.D: Incorrect. Corticosteroids increase susceptibility to infection; infection-prevention behaviours remain essential.

items.stem: Before accessing a central venous catheter hub to administer IV medication, which action best reduces CLABSI risk?

options.text: Vigorously scrub the hub/access port with an appropriate antiseptic and allow it to dry before access.
Wipe the hub once with tap water and connect immediately while still wet with water.
Skip disinfection if the same nurse accessed the line earlier in the shift.
Blow on the hub to dry saliva used as a cleaning agent.

rationales.A: Correct. CDC STRIVE materials direct scrubbing the hub vigorously for at least 5 seconds with an appropriate antiseptic and allowing it to dry prior to every access; OpenStax instructs scrubbing catheter access ports/needleless connectors with chlorhexidine or another approved antiseptic before access and using aseptic technique in CVC maintenance bundles.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Tap water is not an appropriate antiseptic scrub for hub disinfection before access.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Disinfection is required prior to every access, not only the first access of the shift.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Saliva is not an antiseptic; this practice contaminates the hub.

rationales.C: Incorrect. Measles is transmitted via airborne droplet nuclei; Contact-only is incorrect as the keyed precaution set.

items.stem: Which finding is an early symptom the nurse should associate with rising serum sodium (hypernatremia)?

options.text: Thirst.
Complete absence of any fluid or neurologic symptoms in every client with severe hypernatremia.
Sudden productive cough with green sputum as the defining early feature of hypernatremia.
Bright yellow skin as the first and only sign of high sodium.

rationales.C: Incorrect. Productive green sputum suggests pulmonary infection, not the early hallmark of hypernatremia.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Jaundice-like yellow skin is not the early defining sign of hypernatremia.

sources.evidence: The major symptom of hypernatremia is thirst; major signs result from CNS dysfunction due to brain cell shrinkage (confusion, seizures, or coma may result).

verification_log.by: AI author (Composer, Cursor subagent bc-f3bcbe57) — not a licensed clinician
verification_log.result: Key dual-confirmed: OpenStax early thirst in hypernatremia + Merck thirst as major symptom with later CNS signs.
